title: Why Mongolia Is the Emptiest Country on Earth

paragraphs.text: Mongolia sits between Russia and China, and it is huge: more than one and a half million square kilometers, almost three times the size of France. About three and a half million people live there. That makes it the most thinly populated independent country on Earth. And roughly half of those people live in a single city. At night, from orbit, the whole country is one bright dot and a few sparks.

stat.label: Mongolia's area: about 2.8 times metropolitan France (our calculation)
People per square kilometer: the lowest of any sovereign state

paragraphs.text: Mongolia touches only two countries, Russia to the north and China to the south, and it has no coast at all. The nearest sea is hundreds of kilometers away, across China. Its population has grown: from about eight hundred and forty-five thousand at the 1956 census, to about two million in 1989, to about three point three million in 2020. But most of that growth went into towns. Today around seven in ten Mongolians live in cities.

stat.label: Share of Mongolians living in towns and cities, 2023

paragraphs.text: Out there is the coldest capital city in the world, and a lake that holds most of the country's fresh water. There are more horses, sheep, goats, cattle and camels than people, many times over. And in the south, in 1923, explorers dug up the first dinosaur eggs anyone recognized as dinosaur eggs. So why is Mongolia so empty? There are five reasons, and the first is the ground itself: it is too high, too dry and too cold.

shots.on_screen_text: Sheep and goats on the steppe
The red cliffs of Bayanzag from orbit

chapters.title: Too High, Too Dry, Too Cold

paragraphs.text: Reason one. The land is too high, too dry and too cold. The average point in Mongolia stands about one thousand five hundred and eighty meters above the sea. It is about as far from any ocean as you can get. Mountains ring it on the west and north, and the moist air from the seas never makes it this far.

stat.label: Mongolia's average height above sea level

shots.photo: File:Altai Tavan Bogd - Potanin glacier - panoramio.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Potanin glacier, Altai Tavan Bogd

paragraphs.text: So the winters are brutal. In January the average temperature in parts of the country falls to around minus thirty degrees. Ulaanbaatar, at about thirteen hundred meters, is the coldest national capital in the world; across a whole year, its average hovers around freezing. And the sky is clear more than two hundred and fifty days a year.

stat.label: January averages in the coldest parts of Mongolia
Sunny days a year in Mongolia

paragraphs.text: The south is drier still. The Gobi covers much of it, about two fifths of the country by Mongolia's own count. In the Gobi only fifty to a hundred millimeters of rain fall in a year, and some places get none at all for years. Even in the wetter north it is around three hundred. That is less than half of what falls on Paris.

stat.label: Share of Mongolia that is Gobi desert and desert steppe

chart.title: Rain and snow in a year

shots.on_screen_text: Camels below the Khongoryn Els dunes

paragraphs.text: Put cold and dry together and you get a land where very little can be farmed. Less than one percent of Mongolia is arable. Around Ulaanbaatar the ground is free of frost only from about mid-May to late August. And three quarters of the land has already been degraded by drought, overgrazing and wind. In 2026 Mongolia hosted the United Nations conference on desertification.

shots.on_screen_text: Fields near Darkhan, in the north

stat.label: Share of Mongolia's land that is arable

shots.on_screen_text: Hills east of Ulaanbaatar in October

stat.label: Mongolia's land degraded, 2020 national assessment

shots.on_screen_text: An ovoo, a sacred cairn, in the Gobi

paragraphs.text: There is water in the far north. Lake Khövsgöl, up against the Russian border, is about two hundred and sixty-seven meters deep and holds around seventy percent of Mongolia's fresh water. But it sits in larch forest and mountains where the lake freezes over for months. In the far west, the Altai mountains rise to four thousand three hundred and seventy-four meters at Khüiten Peak, and glaciers fill the valleys.

stat.label: Share of Mongolia's fresh water held in Lake Khövsgöl
Khüiten Peak, Mongolia's highest point, in the Altai

paragraphs.text: Even there, people live by animals. In Bayan-Ölgii, the westernmost province, most people are Kazakhs, and some still hunt foxes in winter with trained golden eagles. Since 1999 they have held a Golden Eagle Festival there every autumn. Across the whole country, Kazakhs are about four percent of the population. Everywhere else, the herders are Mongols.

stat.label: The first Golden Eagle Festival, Ölgii
Kazakhs in Mongolia's population, 2020 census

paragraphs.text: And yet the ground was never empty of life. In 1923 an American expedition led by Roy Chapman Andrews reached red cliffs in the Gobi and found nests of fossil eggs, the first that scientists recognized as dinosaur eggs. Andrews called the place the Flaming Cliffs, for the way they glow in the evening sun. One skeleton lay right on top of a nest, and Andrews named the animal Oviraptor, the egg thief, assuming it had died stealing eggs. In 1993 an expedition from the same museum found one sitting on its own nest. It had been brooding its eggs, not robbing them. Those cliffs are sandstone, laid down as dunes in a desert some eighty million years ago. The Gobi was not always a desert. But it has been one for a very long time.

stat.label: The egg thief, named in 1924; in 1993 found brooding its own nest

shots.on_screen_text: Red sandstone badlands of the Gobi

paragraphs.text: Reason two. This land feeds animals, not crops. Where wheat will not grow, grass still does, thin and short, but it covers hundreds of thousands of square kilometers. For thousands of years the people of Mongolia lived the only way that grass allowed: as herders, moving with their animals to fresh pasture with the seasons, carrying their homes with them.

shots.on_screen_text: A herd on the dry steppe

paragraphs.text: That home is the ger, a round tent of felt over a wooden frame that a family can take down in an hour or two and load onto a camel or a truck. Its door traditionally faces south. In summer, families camp near water; in winter, they move to sheltered valleys with pens for the animals. A herd needs room. In a dry year, a family may move many times to find grass, and the pasture is shared, not fenced. A place that feeds people this way can only feed a few of them per square kilometer.

shots.photo: File:The book of Ser Marco Polo - the Venetian concerning the kingdoms and marvels of the East (1903) (14766426971).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Gers on carts, from a 1903 edition of Marco Polo

stat.label: Time a family needs to take down a ger and pack it

The open steppe near the Chinese border

paragraphs.text: And the animals far outnumber the people. At the end of 2023 Mongolia counted about sixty-four point seven million head of livestock. Mongolians call them the five snouts: sheep, goats, cattle, horses and camels. Almost nine in ten were sheep and goats. Even the horses alone outnumber the people. Goats matter most to the herders' cash, because their soft under-hair is sold as cashmere. Mongolia is the world's second-largest producer of raw cashmere, after China. That is roughly twenty animals for every person in the country.

stat.label: Livestock in Mongolia at the end of 2023
stat.source: National Statistics Office of Mongolia, livestock census

shots.on_screen_text: Camels below the Khongoryn Els dunes

stat.source: National Statistics Office of Mongolia, livestock census

shots.on_screen_text: Goat pasture in the Middle Gobi

stat.label: Animals per person in Mongolia, end of 2023 (our calculation)
stat.source: National Statistics Office of Mongolia, livestock census

paragraphs.text: And the herds have been growing. In 2018 the count reached sixty-six and a half million, the most since Mongolia began counting its animals in 1918. More goats mean more cashmere, but goats pull grass up by the roots and cut the soil with their hooves. Overgrazing is one of the main reasons so much of the land is wearing out. In 2018 there were about two hundred and thirty thousand herding households. The steppe can only carry so many animals, and so it can only carry so many herders.

stat.label: Livestock counted in 2018, a record since counting began in 1918
Herding households with livestock, 2018

paragraphs.text: Horses still matter here more than almost anywhere. Every summer at Naadam, the national festival, listed by UNESCO since 2010, Mongolians hold wrestling, archery and horse racing, and children ride horses in races across the open steppe, some of them many kilometers long. It is a country built around animals. But that also means a country that depends, every winter, on the weather.

shots.on_screen_text: A horse in the Orkhon valley

stat.label: Naadam's three contests: wrestling, archery, horse racing

paragraphs.text: Reason three. The winters kill. Mongolians have a word for it: dzud. A dzud comes when a dry summer leaves the animals thin, and then deep snow, ice or extreme cold covers the grass so they cannot reach it. Animals that cannot graze for weeks starve and freeze, by the million. They do not die in one night. They weaken over weeks, and the herders can only watch.

stat.label: A summer drought, then a winter of snow, ice or cold that starves the herds

paragraphs.text: In the winter of 2009 and 2010 more than ten million animals died, about a quarter of all the livestock in the country, according to the United Nations. In 2023 and 2024 it happened again. By late April about seven million animals were dead; a later United Nations assessment put the losses at eight point one million. The national herd fell from sixty-four point seven million to fifty-seven point six million in a single year.

stat.label: Animals killed in the 2009-2010 dzud: about a quarter of all livestock

shots.on_screen_text: A camel lost in a dzud

stat.label: Animals lost in the 2023-2024 dzud (UNDP assessment)

chart.title: Livestock in Mongolia
chart.source: National Statistics Office of Mongolia, livestock census

paragraphs.text: Early forecasts warned that sixteen million animals could die, and the Red Cross launched an emergency appeal. Roads were buried. Families in remote camps ran out of hay and fuel, and aid groups reported children missing school because they were needed to keep the surviving animals alive. In some provinces in the south and east, the losses were worst of all. Dzuds are not new. A run of them from 1999 to 2002 killed millions of animals, and the 2010 dzud was worse. But they now come close together, three hard winters in the last few years alone, and Mongolia's government says the country has warmed by more than two degrees since 1940, faster than most of the world.

stat.label: Animals an early-March 2024 forecast said could die (the final toll was lower)
Worst-hit provinces in spring 2024: Sükhbaatar, Dornogovi, Govisümber, Khentii
Warming in Mongolia since 1940, government figures
stat.source: Mongolia's national communications to the UNFCCC

paragraphs.text: For a herding family, a dzud can wipe out everything they own in a few weeks. A family with no animals has nothing to live on in the countryside. So many of them do what poor rural families everywhere do. They pack up and go to the city. And in Mongolia there is really only one city to go to.

Reason four is history. Eight hundred years ago this was the center of the world. In 1206 a chief named Temüjin took the title Genghis Khan, and his armies built the largest connected land empire there has ever been. At its height it stretched from Korea to Hungary. Its capital, Karakorum, stood in the Orkhon valley. But an empire run from horseback never needed big cities at home, and when it broke up, the herders were still herders.

stat.label: Temüjin takes the title Genghis Khan and founds the Mongol Empire

shots.on_screen_text: Karakorum and the Erdene Zuu monastery

shots.photo: File:The book of Ser Marco Polo - the Venetian concerning the kingdoms and marvels of the East (1903) (14766426971).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Mongol camp, from a 1903 edition of Marco Polo

paragraphs.text: His grandson Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and went on to rule all of China. When that dynasty fell in 1368, the Mongols went back to the steppe. Later the Qing dynasty of China ruled the country for more than two centuries. When the Qing collapsed in 1911, Mongolia declared independence under a Buddhist ruler, the Bogd Khan. In 1921 a revolution backed by Soviet Russia broke away, and in 1924 Mongolia became a people's republic, the first Soviet satellite state. In the late 1930s, under the leader Khorloogiin Choibalsan, a wave of purges killed more than twenty thousand people, among them an estimated seventeen thousand Buddhist monks. In the 1950s the herds were put into state collectives; by 1958 there were seven hundred and twenty-seven of them. Soviet troops stayed in the country until the early 1990s.

paragraphs.text: In the winter of 1989 and 1990 young Mongolians began protesting in the capital. In March 1990 a small group went on hunger strike on the central square. Two days later the ruling party's leadership resigned. It was one of the few revolutions of that year in which nobody was killed.

stat.label: Democratic Union members begin a hunger strike on the main square
The Politburo resigns

paragraphs.text: The Soviets had built towns, mines and a railway, from the Russian border through Ulaanbaatar to China. It reached Ulaanbaatar in 1949 and linked up with Beijing in 1955. Darkhan, an industrial town north of the capital, was founded in 1961, and Erdenet grew up around a huge copper mine. For the first time, many Mongolians lived in apartments and worked in factories. Then in 1990 a peaceful revolution ended one-party rule. In 1991 the collectives were broken up and their animals handed out. With factories closing and jobs disappearing, people went back to the herds: herding households rose from about seventy thousand in 1990 to about two hundred thousand by the end of the decade.

stat.label: A peaceful revolution; the first multiparty elections follow that summer

chart.title: Herding households in Mongolia
chart.source: Yamamura et al., Research Institute for Humanity and Nature

paragraphs.text: Many of those new herders had small flocks and little experience. When the dzuds came, starting in 2000, they were hit hardest. And so the country that had briefly gone back to the steppe started moving to town.

Reason five. Everyone who leaves the land goes to the same place. In its center today, Soviet-era apartment blocks stand next to new glass towers. Ulaanbaatar began in 1639 as a monastery of tents called Örgöö, which moved across the steppe for more than a century and settled in its present valley in 1778. In 1950 about seventy thousand people lived there. By 1989 it was five hundred and forty thousand. By the end of 2022 it was just over one point six million, almost half of the whole country.

The city was planned for about six hundred thousand people, a number it reached in 1990. The newcomers could not afford apartments, so they set up their gers on the hills around it. These ger districts now hold more than half of the city's people, often without running water or sewers. About a third of ger-district households live below the poverty line. To get through winters of minus thirty, they burn raw coal in their stoves.

shots.on_screen_text: Ger districts on the northern hills

stat.label: Share of Ulaanbaatar's people living in ger districts

paragraphs.text: Ulaanbaatar sits in a valley, and in winter cold air gets trapped there under a lid of warmer air. The smoke cannot escape. In the ger districts, the World Bank found that winter levels of fine particles can be more than a hundred times the World Health Organization's daily guideline. Doctors in the city have reported a sharp rise in breathing illnesses, especially among children. One of the coldest capitals on Earth has also become one of the most polluted.

stat.label: Winter fine-particle levels in ger districts against the WHO daily guideline
Rise in respiratory illness per 10,000 people in Ulaanbaatar over a decade

paragraphs.text: The government has tried. In May 2019 it banned burning raw coal in the capital and handed out processed coal briquettes instead. Some winters the air got better. Then the smog came back. In the fifteen years to 2018 the World Bank counted a fifty-five percent rise in the city's population from migration alone, and the newcomers keep coming.

stat.label: Ulaanbaatar bans burning raw coal in homes
Growth in Ulaanbaatar's population from migration over fifteen years

shots.on_screen_text: New ger plots on the eastern edge

paragraphs.text: Mongolia does have wealth. It is under the ground. In the south Gobi, about eighty kilometers from the Chinese border, the Oyu Tolgoi mine produces copper and gold, and Tavan Tolgoi is one of the largest coal deposits in the world. Mining makes up around four fifths of the country's exports, and almost all the coal goes to China, by truck and, since 2022, by a new railway to the border that was expected to cut the cost of moving a ton of coal from forty-seven dollars to twelve. Oyu Tolgoi is owned about two thirds by the mining company Rio Tinto and one third by the Mongolian state. In 2025 the economy grew by almost seven percent, largely on its copper. But a mine needs few people, and it does not need them to stay.

paragraphs.text: So put it together. The land is high, dry and cold, and less than one percent of it can be farmed. What it can do is feed animals, and animals need a lot of room. The winters kill the herds and push the herders out. History built an empire but not cities, and then the collapse of the Soviet system sent people back to the steppe and then into one city. And the wealth that is left is dug out of the ground by a small workforce.

Mongolia is not empty because nobody wants to live there. It is empty because, for most of its history, this land could only support people who kept moving. Next time you see a map of Asia at night, look between Russia and China. That dark square, with one bright dot, is Mongolia. Out on the steppe, a ger may now have a solar panel by the door and a motorbike next to the horses. The herders who remain have not stopped moving. There are just fewer of them every year, and more of their children in the city. Mongolia's emptiness is not a mystery. It is the shape of a hard land, a herding way of life, and a century of history, all pushing people toward one valley.

paragraphs.text: Here is my question for you. If you could spend one year in Mongolia, would you live in a ger on the steppe and move with the herds, or in an apartment in Ulaanbaatar?

shots.on_screen_text: Sheep and goats on the steppe

ask.text: A ger on the steppe, or the city?

youtube.title: Why Mongolia Is the Emptiest Country on Earth
youtube.description: Mongolia is almost three times the size of France, yet about three and a half million people live there, and roughly half of them in one city. This video goes through the five reasons it is the most thinly populated country on Earth: a high, dry, cold land where less than one percent can be farmed, grass that feeds herds rather than crops, the killer winters called dzud, a history that built an empire but no cities and then a Soviet collapse, and the pull of Ulaanbaatar and the mines.
